EOSCore has simple text chat nodes that send messages straight to another player over EOS P2P. They don't need a server, a session or a lobby, only the Product User Id of the other player. This is an EOSCore feature, not an EOS interface, so there is no client policy setting for it.

Custom Invites send an invite with your own text payload to other players, for example the id of a lobby, a party or a server address. Unlike lobby and session invites, EOS does not join anything for you: the receiver reads the payload and joins in your own code.
The Ecom interface handles offers, purchases and entitlements for games sold on the Epic Games Store. It needs an Epic Account login (Auth interface), not only a Connect login.

A lobby is a group of players that share attributes and can talk with voice (RTC) before or during a match. Lobbies are separate from game sessions: a common setup is to gather players in a lobby, then move them to a game session, see Lobby to Session.
The Metrics interface records when a player starts and stops playing. EOS uses it for the player and session statistics in the Developer Portal, such as daily active users and play time.

The Mods interface lists, installs, updates and uninstalls mods that are published for your game on the Epic Games Store. It needs an Epic Account login (Auth interface), and the game must be started from the Epic Games Launcher, which installs the mods.

The P2P interface sends packets directly between players, with NAT traversal and Epic relay servers when a direct connection is not possible. Players are addressed by their Product User Id, no IP addresses or open ports are needed.

The Progression Snapshot interface stores a snapshot of a player's progression on the EOS backend, as a list of key/value text pairs, for example the player's level, character and chapter. EOS uses the snapshots when a player merges several Epic accounts into one: the player sees the progression of each account and picks the one to keep.
These interfaces use Epic Account Services and need an Epic Account login (Auth interface) with the matching permissions (scopes), see Scope Consent.

Online Subsystem interfaces. The EOSCore Online Subsystem now implements IOnlineFriends, IOnlinePresence, IOnlineUser and parts of IOnlineExternalUI. See Supported Platforms and Features. Friends: read the friends list, send, accept and reject friend invites, query blocked players, and get friends list and blocklist notifications. Presence: set and query presence, with presence change notifications. Friend presence is kept in sync. User: query user info and display names, look up users by display name, and query external account mappings. External UI: ShowLoginUI (Account Portal), ShowFriendsUI (EOS overlay), ShowWebURL and OnExternalUIChange. Join from the overlay. Pressing Join on a friend in the EOS social overlay now calls OnSessionUserInviteAccepted with the friend's session. See Join Friends Multiplayer Game. Lobby sessions. With bUseLobbiesIfAvailable the Online Subsystem session interface creates, finds (SEARCH_LOBBIES), joins, updates and leaves EOS Lobbies, with lobby invites, overlay joins, member attributes and participant joined/left notifications. See Lobby Sessions. FindSessionById finds lobbies and EOS sessions by id, and FindFriendSession finds the lobby a friend is in. UpdateSession now applies changes to NumPublicConnections (max players) and bAllowInvites. Platform handle provider. The EOS platform is shared through the EOSPlatformHandleProvider modular feature, so other plugins (such as HostMigrationCore) can use the same EOS platform without depending on EOSCore. See Platform Handle Provider. New settings in the [/Script/OnlineSubsystemEOSCore.EOSCoreSettings] section: SDKLogLevel sets the EOS SDK log level. TaskNetworkTimeoutSeconds sets the network timeout for EOS tasks. See Settings Reference. Connect logout. Logging out of the Online Subsystem now also calls EOS_Connect_Logout. Mobile lifecycle. The EOS application status is set to background suspended or foreground when the app is suspended or resumed.

Platforms: the plugin now lists its supported platforms (PlatformAllowList), so it is no longer loaded on unsupported platforms. -AUTH_TYPE automatic login: credential types now have to match the EOS SDK type names exactly (not case sensitive). An unknown type fails the login instead of picking the wrong credential type. See Command Line Arguments. Blueprint functions called before EOS is initialized, or without a valid platform, now return EOS_NotConfigured instead of failing without a result. Async nodes called without a valid platform now always run their failure output instead of never completing. Multiple worlds: when a world is available (PIE with several clients, for example), the EOSCore subsystem now only uses that world's instance. EOS log messages (ListenForEOSMessages) are now delivered on the game thread. SDK fatal messages are logged as Error, so they no longer crash the game. Configuration overrides: DefaultConfigurationName is only used when no other configuration matches. Settings: bEnabled is now read from the OnlineSubsystemEOSCore settings section. Logging: Access tokens, auth tokens and Web API responses are no longer written to the log. A missing Android or iOS Client Id now gives a build warning. Android: the default AndroidClientId is now empty instead of an example value. Packaging: xaudio2_9redist.dll is staged with the EOS SDK, and the bundled copy is used when the system copy is missing. Error dialog: the dialog for a failed EOS SDK load is no longer shown on dedicated servers, in commandlets or in unattended runs.

Crash when Online Subsystem callbacks ran after their interface had been destroyed, for example during shutdown or a level change. EOS notifications not removed when the Identity and Session interfaces were destroyed. Null dereference in EndSession for LAN sessions. Null dereferences in the Auth and Connect login status changed handlers. Login continuing when the EOS subsystem was missing. Memory leaks in the session invite received and invite accepted handlers. Accepting an invite also checks that the session details could be read. PlayerDataStorage reads and writes sharing the same progress callback. PlayerDataStorage transfer handles that were never released. The EOS platform not being released on shutdown, and the SDK not being shut down last. Wrong EOS cache directory on iOS. A heap allocation for the XAudio DLL path that was never freed. Async action callback signatures that did not match their delegates. Compatibility with newer engine versions in the Build.cs version checks. OnJoinSessionComplete being called twice when joining an EOS session, and a failed join leaving the session behind. The completion delegate passed to DestroySession not being called for EOS sessions. Session invites failing for friends whose Product User Id was not cached by the Identity interface. SEARCH_LOBBIES being sent as a search filter in EOS session searches.

To launch the game you'll now use the EOSBootstrapper.exe file, this should hook your game into Epic Online Services on launch. You can also name the EOSBootstrapper.exe whatever you want in the bootstrapper command above to rename the file to match your project.

Epic Online Services Bootstrapper Tool ++EOSSDK+Release-1.15-CL-20662730. Configures the EOS Bootstrapper for use with an application. This tool performs the following actions: 1. Copies the local Boostrapper executable (EOSBootstrapper.exe) to the output file path (--output-path). 2. (Optional) Updates the program icon and version info of the copied Bootstrapper executable, using the target application executable (--app-path). 3. Creates a new config file next to the output Bootstrapper executable. Usage: EOSBootstrapperTool.exe (-o|--output-path <path>) (-a|--app-path <path>) [-w|--working-dir <path>] [-f|--wait-for-exit [<bool>]] [-n|--no-operation [<bool>]] [-r|--copy-resources [<bool>]] EOSBootstrapperTool.exe [-h|--help] Options: (-o|--output-path <path>) Output file path where to copy the Bootstrapper executable, as a relative or an absolute path, including the file name. (-a|--app-path <path>) Target application file path to run, including relative path if the output Bootstrapper executable will not be located in the same folder. [-w|--working-dir <path>] Optional. Relative working directory to set when running the target application. [-f|--wait-for-exit [<bool>]] Optional, false by default. If set, Bootstrapper will exit only after the target application has exited. [-n|--no-operation [<bool>]] Optional, false by default. If set, the target application will be started directly without initializing the EOS Service. [-r|--copy-resources [<bool>]] Optional, false by default. If set, the program icon and version information is copied into the output Boostrapper executable from the target application executable. This will also remove the existing Authenticode digital signature from the Bootstrapper executable. [-h|--help] Display this help message and exit.
There are several commandline arguments that the plugin can use

-AUTH_TYPE=xxx Logs in the first local player automatically when the Online Subsystem starts, see the supported types below. Not used on dedicated server builds (UE_SERVER). -AUTH_LOGIN=xxx Login Id used by the automatic login, for example the DevTool host address -AUTH_TOKEN=xxx Token or password used by the automatic login. If it is not set, -AUTH_PASSWORD= is used instead (this is what the Epic Games Launcher passes) -EOSConfig=configurationName Use this configuration from Project Settings instead of the Default Configuration Name -epicsandboxid=xxx Overrides the SandboxId of the selected configuration (passed by the Epic Games Launcher) -epicdeploymentid=xxx Overrides the DeploymentId of the selected configuration -EpicPortal Tells the plugin the game was started by the Epic Games Launcher, this enables the Online Subsystem Store/Purchase interface -DisableEOSOverlay Disables the EOS overlay (same as bDisableEOSOverlay in Project Settings) -Port=xxxx Game port. The Online Subsystem writes it to the session as the ServerPort attribute so clients connect to the right port

The value is not case sensitive. An unknown value makes the automatic login fail with an error in the log. AUTH_TYPE Login method devtool or developer DevTool, AUTH_LOGIN is the DevTool host (localhost:1111), AUTH_TOKEN is the credential name persistentauth or autologin Previously saved login on this computer (Persistent Auth) portal or accountportal Account Portal (EOS overlay or browser) exchangecode Exchange code, used when started from the Epic Games Launcher deviceid DeviceId, AUTH_LOGIN is the display name password Email and password (restricted by Epic, not generally available) devicecode Device code refreshtoken Refresh token external or externalauth External auth

Logging in to your instance of DevTool at localhost:1111 "C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.6\Engine\Binaries\Win64\UnrealEditor.exe" "C:\EOSProject\EOSProject.uproject" -game -log -AUTH_TYPE=devtool -AUTH_LOGIN=localhost:1111 -AUTH_TOKEN=MrX

EOSCore was primarily made with Blueprints in mind and is not convenient to use in a C++ environment, there is also no benefit to using EOSCore in a C++ environment compared to Blueprints, however it is totally doable. This example will show you a basic implementation and how to get started but also note that if you decide to use EOSCore in C++ you will be on your own. If you are having issues compiling your C++ project then you will have to solve the issues on your own. One of the reason for this is C++ is extremely complicated and complex and not what the plugin is advertised or even suggested to be used with. With that out of the way, let’s get started!

Open up your projects \Source\Project\Project.Build.cs file and add EOSCore as a module dependency. If you also use the Online Subsystem classes directly (for example FOnlineSubsystemEOSCore), add OnlineSubsystemEOSCore and OnlineSubsystem as well. Here is an example of what a Build.cs file can look like that includes the EOSCore module

using UnrealBuildTool; public class MyProject : ModuleRules { public MyProject(ReadOnlyTargetRules Target) : base(Target) { PCHUsage = PCHUsageMode.UseExplicitOrSharedPCHs; PublicDependencyModuleNames.AddRange(new string[] { "Core", "CoreUObject", "Engine", "InputCore", "EOSCore" }); } }

We’re going to setup a basic test function that will attempt to Login using the EOS Connect Interface with a DeviceId. A DeviceId has to be created once per device before it can be used to login, so the example first calls EOS_Connect_CreateDeviceId and then logs in. If the DeviceId already exists, CreateDeviceId returns EOS_DuplicateNotAllowed, which is fine. note All EOSCore callbacks are executed on the game thread from the EOS tick. If the plugin is not initialized (no EOS platform), the callback is called right away with EOS_NotConfigured. Here is an example of the Header and Source files:

#pragma once #include "CoreMinimal.h" #include "Connect/EOSConnectTypes.h" #include "GameFramework/PlayerController.h" #include "BaseController.generated.h" UCLASS() class ABaseController : public APlayerController { GENERATED_BODY() public: UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "EOS TEST") void MyTestFunction(); public: UFUNCTION() void OnCreateDeviceIdCallback(const FEOSConnectCreateDeviceIdCallbackInfo& Data); UFUNCTION() void OnLoginCallback(const FEOSConnectLoginCallbackInfo& Data); private: void Login(); public: FOnCreateDeviceIdCallback m_OnCreateDeviceIdCallback; FOnLoginCallback m_OnLoginCallback; };

#include "BaseController.h" #include "Connect/EOSConnect.h" void ABaseController::MyTestFunction() { if (UCoreConnect* Connect = UCoreConnect::GetConnect(this)) { m_OnCreateDeviceIdCallback.BindUFunction(this, "OnCreateDeviceIdCallback"); FEOSConnectCreateDeviceIdOptions Options; Options.DeviceModel = "PC Windows"; Connect->EOSConnectCreateDeviceId(this, Options, m_OnCreateDeviceIdCallback); } } void ABaseController::OnCreateDeviceIdCallback(const FEOSConnectCreateDeviceIdCallbackInfo& Data) { // EOS_DuplicateNotAllowed means a DeviceId already exists on this device if (Data.ResultCode == EOSResult::EOS_Success || Data.ResultCode == EOSResult::EOS_DuplicateNotAllowed) { Login(); } } void ABaseController::Login() { if (UCoreConnect* Connect = UCoreConnect::GetConnect(this)) { m_OnLoginCallback.BindUFunction(this, "OnLoginCallback"); FEOSConnectLoginOptions Options; Options.UserLoginInfo.DisplayName = "Test"; Options.Credentials.Type = EEOSEExternalCredentialType::EOS_ECT_DEVICEID_ACCESS_TOKEN; Connect->EOSConnectLogin(this, Options, m_OnLoginCallback); } } void ABaseController::OnLoginCallback(const FEOSConnectLoginCallbackInfo& Data) { if (Data.ResultCode == EOSResult::EOS_Success) { // Login successful } else if (Data.ResultCode == EOSResult::EOS_InvalidUser) { // First login with this DeviceId: create the EOS user with EOS_Connect_CreateUser and Data.ContinuanceToken } else { // Login failed } } Now it’s simply a matter of calling the test function from Blueprints

This guide explains how to properly leave a multiplayer session in Unreal Engine using the EOSCore plugin. Failing to clean up a session correctly can prevent players from joining new sessions or cause network conflicts.

You must always call the DestroySession node when leaving a session — whether by player choice, or disconnection. Failing to do so will: Leave the session registered with Epic Online Services (EOS). Prevent the player from joining any new session until the game restarts. Cause "Session already exists" or "Join failed" errors.

The DestroySession node can be called from anywhere in your game: Player Controller (recommended for player-initiated leave) Game Instance (ideal for global cleanup) UI Widget (on "Leave Game" button press) It does not matter where — only that it is called. Important: What DestroySession does depends on who calls it. On a client it only removes the session locally, the host and the other players are not affected. On the host (the session owner) it removes the session from EOS, so it no longer shows up in searches. See Host Leaving below.
[Player Clicks "Leave Game"] ↓ DestroySession ↓ (On Success) Open Level → "MainMenu"
Scenario Call DestroySession? Player leaves via menu Yes Disconnected by host/kick Yes Network timeout Yes Returning to main menu Yes

Call on Level Transition: Use Event End Play or On Destroyed in your Player Controller to ensure cleanup. Handle Disconnections: Bind to OnNetworkFailure or OnSessionFailure events to auto-destroy. UI Feedback: Show "Leaving session..." while DestroySession completes. Error Handling: Even if DestroySession fails, proceed to the menu, but log the error. The local session stays registered until it is destroyed or the game restarts, so call DestroySession again before creating or joining a new session.

Problem Cause Fix "Cannot join session" Old session not destroyed Call DestroySession Stuck in "Joining..." Session cleanup skipped Add DestroySession on leave Multiple sessions in EOS Dashboard Players not cleaning up Enforce DestroySession

Host Leaving: The rule above applies to players leaving. The host calls DestroySession only when the whole game ends, because it removes the session for everyone. To stop the match but keep the session, use EndSession instead. Testing: Use Standalone Game instances to verify cleanup in logs. Remember: DestroySession = Mandatory for clean session lifecycle.

This guide explains how to set or override the maximum number of players (MaxPlayers) for your Unreal Engine game session using the GameSession settings in your configuration files.
documents.s: Configuring Max Players for Game Sessions

documents.t: The default value for MaxPlayers is defined in the Engine\Config\BaseGame.ini file: [/Script/Engine.GameSession] MaxPlayers=16 This sets the default maximum number of players to 16 for a game session unless overridden.

To customize the MaxPlayers value for your game, you can override the default setting by adding or modifying the following in your project’s Config\DefaultGame.ini file: [/Script/Engine.GameSession] MaxPlayers=64

Open DefaultGame.ini: Locate your project’s DefaultGame.ini file in the Config directory (e.g., YourProject/Config/DefaultGame.ini). Add or Update the Setting: Under the [/Script/Engine.GameSession] section, set MaxPlayers to your desired value (e.g., 64). If the section doesn’t exist, create it and add the line. Save and Apply: Save the DefaultGame.ini file. Restart the Unreal Editor or rebuild your project to apply the changes.
Scope: The MaxPlayers setting applies to the game session and affects the maximum number of players that can join a multiplayer session or server.

We begin by listening for the callback Get ticket for Web Api Response before calling the Get Auth Ticket for Web Api function, note the Identifier here is the same one we defined earlier, in this example "STEAMCORE". On callback we unbind the event so it does not fire the Login node multiple times later in the project when we try to refresh login tokens, then call the Login node using the Ticket.

EOS login tokens have an expiration time (currently 60 minutes at the time of writing this article), which means they need to be refreshed every ~60 minutes. The EOS SDK will let us know when this needs to happen so all we have to do is listen for that by adding the EOS_Connect_AddNotifyAuthExpiration function and then provide the Online Subsystem with our new Steam Session Ticket. Use the Update Steam Session Ticket function to update the cached session ticket in the online subsystem module, which the plugin will use to refresh the login token. This guide provides instructions for configuring the EOS Online Subsystem in your project. Proper configuration is essential for establishing network connectivity and multiplayer functionality.

Important Before proceeding, verify that your DefaultEngine.ini file does not contain any duplicate entries for the configurations listed below. Duplicate entries will cause configuration conflicts and prevent proper functionality.
For a visual walkthrough of this process, please refer to our Video Tutorial.
Navigate to your project's configuration directory and open the DefaultEngine.ini file located at: Project\Config\DefaultEngine.ini

Add the following configuration to your DefaultEngine.ini file. Ensure that you update the DefaultPlatformService to use EOSCore instead of any previously configured service (such as Steam). [OnlineSubsystem] DefaultPlatformService=EOSCore [/Script/OnlineSubsystemEOSCore.NetDriverEOSCore] NetConnectionClassName="/Script/OnlineSubsystemEOSCore.NetConnectionEOSCore" bIsUsingP2PSockets=true [/Script/Engine.GameEngine] !NetDriverDefinitions=ClearArray +NetDriverDefinitions=(DefName="GameNetDriver",DriverClassName="/Script/OnlineSubsystemEOSCore.NetDriverEOSCore",DriverClassNameFallback="/Script/OnlineSubsystemUtils.IpNetDriver") [EOSSDK] bHasProjectBinary=true This configuration makes EOSCore the default Online Subsystem and routes game traffic through EOS P2P (NAT traversal and relay servers) using the EOSCore NetDriver. The [EOSSDK] bHasProjectBinary=true entry makes the engine's own EOS modules use the EOS SDK binary that ships with EOSCore, so the two never load different SDK versions. Your EOS credentials (ProductId, SandboxId, DeploymentId, ClientId, ClientSecret, EncryptionKey) are set in Project Settings > Plugins > EOSCore Plugin, see Project Settings Reference.

To optimize network performance, you may configure additional settings for the NetDriverEOSCore. These settings help manage data transmission rates between clients and servers, preventing network congestion that can occur with high frame rate applications. Benefits​ Prevents clients from overwhelming servers with excessive data packets Establishes consistent communication rates regardless of application frame rate Reduces packet loss due to network saturation Configuration​ [/Script/OnlineSubsystemEOSCore.NetDriverEOSCore] NetConnectionClassName="/Script/OnlineSubsystemEOSCore.NetConnectionEOSCore" MaxNetTickRate=60 NetServerMaxTickRate=60 LanServerMaxTickRate=60 NetClientTicksPerSecond=60 bClampListenServerTickRates=true MaxClientRate=100000 MaxInternetClientRate=100000

MaxNetTickRate: Maximum network update frequency (60 Hz recommended) NetServerMaxTickRate: Server-side maximum tick rate LanServerMaxTickRate: LAN-specific maximum tick rate NetClientTicksPerSecond: Client-side network update frequency bClampListenServerTickRates: Enables rate limiting for listen servers MaxClientRate: Maximum data rate for client connections (bytes per second) MaxInternetClientRate: Maximum data rate for internet-based connections
For detailed explanations of individual network settings and advanced configuration options, please consult the official engine documentation.

This guide provides step-by-step instructions for installing the EOSCore plugin through the Epic Games Launcher. The plugin enables Epic Online Services functionality within your Unreal Engine project.
For a visual walkthrough of the installation process, please refer to our Video Tutorial.

Before installing the EOSCore plugin, you must disable the default EOS plugins that are included with the Unreal Engine. These built-in plugins will conflict with the EOSCore plugin and cause functionality issues. Required Actions: Open your project and go to Edit > Plugins Search for EOS Disable the engine-provided EOS plugins (Online Subsystem EOS, EOS Shared, EOS Voice Chat, Socket Subsystem EOS) as shown below, then restart the editor Critical Step Failure to disable the engine's default EOS plugins will result in plugin conflicts and prevent proper functionality. Some engine plugins depend on EOS Shared and enable it again. If you have to keep EOS Shared enabled, add [EOSSDK] bHasProjectBinary=true to your DefaultEngine.ini (see Configuring Online Subsystem) so the engine uses the EOS SDK binary that ships with EOSCore. The editor log warns about this when one of these plugins is enabled.

Open the Epic Games Launcher Go to Fab Library (the plugin is sold on Fab) Search for the EOSCore plugin Click Install to Engine to begin the installation process Gumroad If you bought the plugin on Gumroad, unzip it into your project's Plugins folder instead, so you get YourProject/Plugins/EOSCore/EOSCore.uplugin.

A dialog will appear prompting you to select your target engine version Choose the appropriate Unreal Engine version (e.g., 4.27 as shown in the example) Click Install to proceed with the installation The Epic Games Launcher will automatically download and install the plugin for your selected engine version.

After the installation process completes, verify that the plugin has been successfully installed: Check the plugin status in the Epic Games Launcher Confirm the plugin appears in your engine's plugin list Verify the installation was completed without errors
Once the plugin installation is verified, you can proceed to enable the EOSCore plugin in your Unreal Engine project and begin configuration as outlined in the subsequent documentation sections.

If you encounter issues during installation: Ensure you have properly disabled all engine EOS plugins Verify you have sufficient disk space for the installation Check that your Epic Games Launcher is up to date Restart the launcher if the installation appears to hang For additional support, consult the official plugin documentation or community forums.

This guide outlines the recommended process for updating the EOSCore plugin. Due to limitations in the Epic Games Launcher's plugin update mechanism, a clean reinstallation is the preferred method to ensure proper functionality and avoid potential conflicts.

The Epic Games Launcher's plugin update feature may not always properly handle plugin updates, which can result in: Incomplete file replacements Residual configuration conflicts Compatibility issues with newer versions Corrupted plugin installations To avoid these issues, we recommend performing a complete uninstall and reinstall process.
Open the Epic Games Launcher Navigate to your Engine version's plugin section Click on Installed Plugins for your specific Engine version

Locate the EOSCore plugin in your installed plugins list Click the Remove button to uninstall the plugin Confirm the uninstallation when prompted Allow the Epic Games Launcher to complete the uninstallation process.

For a thorough cleanup, manually verify that all plugin files have been removed: Navigate to your Unreal Engine installation directory Access the following path (replace 4.27 with your engine version): C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_4.27\Engine\Plugins\Marketplace\EOSCore If the EOSCore folder still exists, delete it manually Empty the Recycle Bin to ensure complete removal Best Practice Manual file cleanup helps prevent potential conflicts that may arise from incomplete automatic uninstallation.
Once the cleanup process is complete: Follow the standard plugin installation procedure Ensure you select the correct engine version during installation Verify the installation completed successfully

After reinstalling the plugin: Project Compatibility: Open your existing projects and verify the plugin loads correctly Configuration Check: Review your plugin settings to ensure they match your previous configuration Functionality Test: Test core plugin features to confirm proper operation

If you encounter issues during the update process: Plugin Not Uninstalling: Restart the Epic Games Launcher and try again Manual Deletion Required: Use administrator privileges if you cannot delete plugin files Installation Fails: Ensure you have sufficient disk space and proper permissions Project Errors: Check that the plugin is properly enabled in your project settings

While clean installation is recommended, you may also consider: Engine Update: Updating your entire Unreal Engine installation Direct Download: Obtaining the latest plugin version directly from the developer (if available) However, these methods may not provide the same level of reliability as the clean installation approach.
After installing the plugin and enabling it for your project you can start using EOS functionality!
